# Overview

This is a short answer assignment that's practice for writing an essay. You'll answer four short answer questions. Collectively, your answers will be in the basic form of an essay. When we do essays in November, you'll hopefully go through the same steps without the prompts.

That said, this is **not** an essay. You're answering four questions. There are going to be four windows in Canvas to write the answers into. They are graded separately. You don't need to put an introduction or a conclusion around them. (Though hopefully once you've written your answers, you can see what kind of introduction and conclusion you would write.)

**Pick one of the two options below and answer all four questions about it.** You should be answering four questions here; not eight. You don't have to do both options. But do pick one option and stick to it.

# The four questions

1.  **State the view**, in your own words. What exactly is it claiming? *About 150 words.*

2.  **Give the strongest argument its defenders offer.** Don't offer a barrage here; pick the argument you think is best and set it out. Ideally, make it visible where the possible points of disagreement are. *About 250 words.*

3.  **State the objection you find most serious.** Again, don't run through a barrage of objections; make one objection, and make it well.  *About 250 words.*

4.  **Give the best reply available to the view's defender**. Also, **say whether and why you think that succeeds**. This is the hardest part, because it asks you to argue against yourself. In question 3 you were trying to make the objection as strong as you could. Here you have to take that same argument and find where it goes wrong. If you decide it doesn't go wrong anywhere, and the defender has no good answer, still say what the best of the bad lot of replies is, and why it doesn't work. What you shouldn't do is quietly make the objection weaker here than it was in question 3, so that the reply has an easier time of it. *About 350 words.*

That's about 1000 words in total. These are guides, not limits; and in some cases you can do the job crisply in fewer words. That's good, if you can manage it.

The range of acceptable answers gets broader as the questions go along. In question 1, there is more or less an objective fact about what the view says. But there's a range of good arguments for it, a bigger range of objections, and because there are multiple replies to each objection, you have many many choices by question 4. You are graded on how well you present the arguments, not on whether these are right or wrong, or whether they are the views we agree with. The questions have been chosen so that by question 4, there are many ways to take either side of the debate and get full marks.

# Option A: The knowledge argument

**The view.** Physicalism is false. There are truths about experience that no amount of physical information captures. This is Frank Jackson's conclusion in "What Mary Didn't Know," and his argument for it rests on the Mary case.

**Where to look.** The two readings for lecture 12. Jackson's paper gives the argument in his own words, and the three numbered lines in it are key to Q2. Kıymaz's "The Knowledge Argument Against Physicalism" sets out the standard responses one section at a time, and essential reading for Q3. He covers  the ability hypothesis (§1), the acquaintance hypothesis (§2), the phenomenal concept strategy (§3), and the objection that Mary learns nothing at all (§4).

We skipped acquiantance in class, but it's fine to use here if you think it's the best move. You can also raise objections of your own, though do tell us where you got it from if you got it from elsewhere.

# Option B: Representationalism about perception

**The view.** Perceptual experience represents the world as being a certain way, much as a sentence does. Looking at the checkerboard, your experience represents square A as darker than square B. Representations can be false; that's what happens in illusions. But nothing needs to be darker for the experience to represent the square as darker. At the end of lecture 10 this was flagged briefly as a rival to Russell's sense-data theory.

**A note on the name.** Philosophers also call this view *intentionalism*, and the encyclopedia entry below uses that name throughout rather than "representationalism". But it's the same view, just names that are more popular with different folks.

**Where to look.** We really skimmed this in lecture, and Russell doesn't discuss it, so if you take this option three sections that were listed as recommended become required. All three are in Tim Crane and Craig French, ["The Problem of Perception"](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/perception-problem/), in the *Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy*.

- **§2.1, The Argument from Illusion.** This is what Q3 is about.
- **§3.3.1, Intentionalism in Outline.** This will be really helpful for Q1.
- **§3.3.4, Intentionalism and the Problem of Perception.** Your answer to Q4 should draw on this.

You do not need the rest of §3.3.

For Q2, the case for this view is mostly a case against its rival: the sense-data view we discussed. So the problems for sense-data, whether we have shared evidence, whether we can know about the world, what kind of objects sense-data are, are all available moves here. Paul Coates, ["Sense-Data"](https://iep.utm.edu/sense-da/), in the *Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy*, sorts the objections into three kinds in §4. That's still recommended, but it's a natural place to start.
